title: Not too much
hook: Montaigne distrusts extremes, even in virtue

segments.voice: Yesterday, the essay as a practice: Montaigne's essays are trials, a stick pushed into the river. Your line was a trying-out. What small experiment did you run? Day one thousand one hundred eighty.

A friend starts running. Good. Then it's every morning, then twice a day, then the knees give out and the running stops completely. Another friend decides to be honest, really honest, and within a week has told three people exactly what's wrong with their haircuts, their marriages and their cooking. The goal was good both times. Something went wrong anyway. Montaigne has an essay about exactly this, and it says something unexpected: you can hold even a virtue too tightly. Today, not too much.
screen: `RUNNING, THEN TOO MUCH RUNNING.` → `HONEST, THEN TOO HONEST.` → `A VIRTUE HELD TOO TIGHTLY.`

segments.voice: First, the image. In the essay Of moderation, Montaigne says it's as if our touch were infectious. We take hold of things that are good in themselves and spoil them by how we handle them. Second, the claim. We can grip virtue so hard, he says, with such violent desire, that it turns into a fault. He knows the objection: some say there can't be too much virtue, because once it's excessive it isn't virtue anymore. Montaigne calls that playing with words. In real life, people do overdo good things. Third, his witness. He points to a line of Saint Paul, from the letter to the Romans. In the King James Bible it reads: "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly." Montaigne hears in it a call to be wise with measure, not to push even wisdom past its proper size. Fourth, what this asks of us. Not to care less. Montaigne isn't asking anyone to be lukewarm about being kind or honest or healthy. He's asking for a grip that doesn't crush what it holds. Honesty that still leaves the other person standing. Discipline that still leaves the knees working. Devotion that still leaves room for dinner with friends. In a normal week, it might look like stopping one step before the point where the good thing starts turning sour, and trusting that the good thing will still be there tomorrow.
screen: `AS IF OUR TOUCH WERE INFECTIOUS.` · `VIRTUE GRIPPED TOO HARD.` · `THINK SOBERLY.` · `A GRIP THAT DOESN'T CRUSH.` · then, large: `NOT TOO MUCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go moderate on one thing. Sit, and notice your hands. Are they clenched at all? Let them loosen. Now bring to mind one good thing you've been gripping hard lately: work, a diet, a cause, helping someone, being right. Don't drop it. Just imagine holding it the way you'd hold a bird, firmly enough that it stays, gently enough that it breathes. Notice what changes in your shoulders. The bell holds the time.
Not too much. In Of moderation, Montaigne warns that we can grip even a virtue so hard it turns into a fault. Today's word.
Your line: not too much. Today, pick one good thing you tend to overdo, and stop one step earlier than usual. Day one thousand one hundred eighty.

howItsDone: In the essay Of moderation, Montaigne argues that even good things, virtue included, can be spoiled by being grasped too violently, and he appeals to Saint Paul's call to think soberly.

fork.setup: someone tells Montaigne: excess virtue isn't virtue, so you can't have too much of it. what does he say?
options: that's playing with words; people really do overdo good things.
fork.reveal: he calls it playing with words. in real life, he says, we can seize virtue so violently that it becomes a fault.

original.note: Montaigne's French title for the essay Of moderation.

what it means: Montaigne asks for a grip on good things that doesn't crush them, even on virtue.
what a scholar hears: he answers the objection that excess virtue isn't virtue by calling it wordplay, and he leans on Romans 12:3 for wisdom held with measure.
